title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
wiki: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
note: A Civil War poster in which a red triangle, the Bolsheviks, pierces a white circle, the counter-revolutionary Whites. Politics told in pure geometry.

title: Monument to the Third International
note: Designed as a spiralling iron headquarters for the Communist International, taller than the Eiffel Tower. It was never built; only models survive.

title: Lenin Tribune
note: A design for a slanting steel speaker’s platform for Lenin, raised above the crowd on a lattice tower.

title: Liberty Leading the People
note: Painted to commemorate the July Revolution in Paris: Liberty leads workers, students and a boy over the barricade.

title: The Third of May 1808
note: Napoleon’s soldiers executing Spanish civilians. It is often called the first modern painting of the victims of war.

title: The Disasters of War
note: Eighty-two prints recording atrocities during the Peninsular War. They were too dangerous to publish until 1863, decades after Goya’s death.

title: The Stone Breakers
note: Two road labourers painted life-size, a scale once reserved for kings and gods. The canvas was destroyed in Dresden in 1945.

title: The Gleaners
note: Three peasant women gathering the leftovers of someone else’s harvest. Conservative critics saw dangerous sympathy for the rural poor.

title: The Third-Class Carriage
note: Daumier, once jailed for caricaturing the king, painted the tired dignity of working people riding in the cheapest railway seats.

title: The Potato Eaters
note: Van Gogh wanted to show peasants eating with the same hands that had dug the potatoes from the earth.

title: Barge Haulers on the Volga
note: Eleven men harnessed like animals, dragging a barge upriver. It made Repin famous across Europe.

title: A Weavers’ Revolt
note: Six prints on the 1844 Silesian weavers’ uprising. The Kaiser vetoed a gold medal the series had been nominated for.

title: In Memoriam Karl Liebknecht
note: Kollwitz’s woodcut of workers mourning over Liebknecht’s body after his murder in 1919.

title: The Fourth Estate
note: Striking peasants advancing calmly toward the viewer, led by a man and a woman holding a child. It became the emblem of the Italian labour movement.

title: La Calavera Catrina
note: A skeleton in a fancy French hat: Posada’s jab at Mexicans who aped European aristocracy while the poor went hungry.

title: The Slave Ship
note: Enslaved people thrown overboard into a storm, recalling the Zong massacre. Turner showed it the year of a great anti-slavery convention in London.

title: Am I Not a Man and a Brother?
wiki: Am I Not a Man and a Brother?
note: The emblem of British abolitionism, mass-produced as medallions and worn on bracelets and hatpins.

title: Peterloo print
note: Carlile, who was on the hustings that day, published this print of the cavalry charge and was jailed for his radical publishing.

title: Breaker boys
note: Hine photographed children sorting coal in Pennsylvania for the National Child Labor Committee, and his pictures helped win child labour laws.

title: Migrant Mother
note: Florence Owens Thompson, a destitute pea picker in California, photographed for the Resettlement Administration. It became the face of the Depression.

title: We Can Do It!
note: Made for Westinghouse factory workers in wartime, it was forgotten until the women’s movement adopted it in the 1980s.

title: Haymarket Martyrs’ Monument
note: A woman places a wreath on a fallen worker, over the graves of the executed Haymarket anarchists near Chicago.

title: The Communards’ Wall
note: The wall in Père Lachaise cemetery where 147 Communards were shot in the last days of the Paris Commune. It has been a site of pilgrimage ever since.

title: Battleship Potemkin
note: A silent film on the 1905 mutiny whose Odessa Steps massacre sequence is still studied in film schools.

title: Worker and Kolkhoz Woman
note: A giant steel worker and farm woman raising hammer and sickle, built for the Soviet pavilion at the 1937 Paris fair.

title: Man at the Crossroads
note: Commissioned for Rockefeller Center and destroyed because Rivera put Lenin in it. He repainted it in Mexico City.

title: Detroit Industry Murals
note: Twenty-seven panels in the Detroit Institute of Arts honouring the workers of Ford’s River Rouge plant.

title: Guernica
note: Picasso’s response to the bombing of the Basque town by German and Italian aircraft supporting Franco.

title: The Passion of Sacco and Vanzetti
wiki: The Passion of Sacco and Vanzetti
note: Shahn painted the two executed anarchists in their coffins, watched over by the men who sealed their fate.

title: The Migration Series
note: Sixty panels on the Great Migration of Black Americans from the rural South to the industrial North.

title: Salt of the Earth
note: A film about a zinc miners’ strike in New Mexico, made by blacklisted Hollywood workers with the miners and their families as cast.

title: Hiroshima Panels
note: Fifteen huge folding screens painted by a married couple who walked into Hiroshima days after the bombing.

title: Peace symbol
note: Designed for the first Aldermaston march against nuclear weapons, from the semaphore signals for N and D.

title: Raised fist
note: A salute of solidarity carried by the IWW, the antifascists of the 1930s, the Black Power movement and many more.

title: The Problem We All Live With
wiki: The Problem We All Live With
note: Six-year-old Ruby Bridges walking between US marshals to integrate a New Orleans school in 1960.

title: Wall of Respect
note: An outdoor mural of Black heroes on Chicago’s South Side that launched the community mural movement.

title: Tucumán Arde
note: Artists and sociologists exposed the dictatorship’s ruin of Tucumán’s sugar workers in a show held at a union hall.

title: Atelier Populaire
note: During May 1968, the occupied fine-arts school printed hundreds of anonymous silkscreen posters for the strikes overnight.

title: OSPAAAL posters
artist: Organization of Solidarity with the Peoples of Asia, Africa and Latin America
note: Havana’s solidarity posters were folded into copies of Tricontinental magazine and mailed around the world.

title: The Black Panther newspaper art
note: The Panthers’ Minister of Culture filled the paper’s back pages with bold drawings of community self-defence and survival programs.

title: Taller de Gráfica Popular
note: A Mexico City workshop that made cheap linocut posters and broadsides for unions, peasants and antifascists.

title: Serigraphs for peace and justice
note: A nun and printmaker who turned pop-art lettering and grocery slogans into silkscreens for civil rights and against the Vietnam War.

title: Chicano Park murals
note: Residents occupied land under the Coronado Bridge in 1970 and covered its pillars with murals. It is now a National Historic Landmark.

title: Balmy Alley murals
note: A San Francisco alley of murals, many painted in the 1980s against US intervention in Central America.

title: Silence = Death
note: A pink triangle on black, reclaimed from the Nazi camps, became the image of AIDS activism.
